description: SOIL-TO-SKY ROBO TEAM will build a farmer-friendly system combining NASA POWER, SMAP, IMERG and NDVI data with field sensor readings and farmer priorities to rank rotation plans under climate scenarios. We'll spend the weekend on NASA data and decision logic. Seeking: remote-sensing/Python person, agronomist, ML/data scientist, UI designer, storyteller. Bring curiosity and follow-through.
summary: RotaShift is an open-source decision-support tool that helps farmers in Bangladesh compare three-season crop rotations under a changing climate. For a chosen field it combines NASA POWER climate data, soil pH and fertility class, crop water use and BARC nutrient recommendations with the farmer's priorities (water saving, soil health, income, resilience). It ranks 72 rotations built from 13 locally grown crops, shows each crop's water deficit and nutrient needs, lets users test warming and rainfall scenarios, and reports how stable the top recommendation is. NASA SMAP soil moisture and MODIS NDVI add satellite context, and our Farmbot field sensors are designed to ground-truth them. It answers Field Shift by turning NASA Earth observations and local soil information into clear, explainable rotation choices.
details:
What it does: Ranks crop-rotation plans for a selected site and shows, for the best plan, crop water use vs effective rainfall, irrigation need, dry-spell length, BARC nutrient recommendations for the chosen soil fertility class, climate-scenario effects and a Monte Carlo stability check.

How it works: A Python/Streamlit app pulls daily NASA POWER temperature, rainfall and humidity, converts rainfall to effective rainfall (USDA-SCS method) and scores every rotation (one crop per rabi, kharif-1 and kharif-2 slot) on climate fit, water efficiency, soil health (legumes, root diversity, no rice monoculture), relative income and resilience, weighted by farmer priorities. SMAP soil moisture and MODIS NDVI exported through Google Earth Engine are shown as context. Scripts calibrate Farmbot soil-moisture probes and compare them with SMAP.

Benefits: A transparent, explainable way for smallholders to compare rotations that save water and protect soil; adaptable to other regions by swapping the crop and nutrient tables.

What we hope to achieve: Validate against field sensors at two Bangladesh sites, add plot-level GPS, HLS 30 m NDVI and IMERG rainfall, and test with local farmers and agronomists.

Tools: Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, Google Earth Engine, NASA POWER API; hardware from our prior-work Farmbot (ESP32 sensors, Raspberry Pi, YOLOv8).

Limitations: Rule-based guidance, not yield forecasts. Reference water data come from other regions; four crops use FAO-56 planning estimates. Only one BARC yield group is loaded per rice crop. SMAP values carry the product's not-recommended quality flag and 9 km pixels show trends only; NDVI is cloud-masked in the monsoon. Coordinates are approximate. Sensor validation against SMAP is [pending / results: n=__, RMSE=__]. No disease detection is claimed.
